analysis.one_liner: Limits the number of patents brand biologic makers can use to sue cheaper competitors in court.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill unanimously in July 2024, but the House never voted on it, so it died at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When a drug company's patent is about to expire, cheaper copycat versions called generics or biosimilars should come to market. Brand-name makers sometimes fight these competitors by stacking dozens of patents into lawsuits that drag on for years. This bill would limit the number of patents a biologic maker can sue with, so cheaper versions reach patients sooner. The Senate passed it with no dissent, but only after stripping out the part that would have banned 'product hopping' — a brand company's trick of switching patients to a slightly changed version of a drug to reset its patent clock. The House never voted, and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs — medicines for conditions like arthritis, cancer, and diabetes. By limiting how many patents a brand company can pile into a lawsuit against a biosimilar maker, the bill makes it harder to keep cheaper copies off the market for years, which would lower drug prices. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers benefit from less costly litigation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high biologic drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Caps at 20 the number of patents a brand biologic maker can pile into one lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant, with at most 10 filed more than four years after the original approval — limiting one common tactic for stretching out a monopoly.

When a biosimilar maker completes the required FDA pathway steps, the brand company's patent litigation is limited, with exceptions only for good cause shown to a court, so generics reach the market sooner.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, whose ability to delay biosimilar competition through long patent litigation would be curtailed, potentially reducing their monopoly-era revenues.

drawbacks.text: The version the Senate passed was stripped down: it no longer includes the original product-hopping ban or FTC enforcement authority, and limits only the number of patents a biologic maker can assert in a biosimilar lawsuit, with court-created exceptions and waivers.
The patent cap applies only to biologics and only when a biosimilar maker completes the full regulatory pathway, and courts can raise the cap for good cause, which industry litigants will test.
The bill fills the Medicare Improvement Fund with $1.8 billion, a relatively small provision whose relationship to the bill's drug-price subject matter is thin.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Even the weaker Senate-passed version would help patients by making it harder to bury biosimilar competitors under dozens of patent lawsuits, at essentially no cost to taxpayers. The honest objection is that the version that advanced is narrow: it caps only the count of patents asserted in litigation and covers only biologics, so brand companies retain other tools to delay generics, and it dies with the House taking no action.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, but the House never voted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably in February 2023 and it was placed on the Senate calendar in March 2023.

On July 11, 2024, the Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent, but the version passed had been amended so that only the patent-limiting provision for biosimilars remained; the original product-hopping ban and FTC enforcement authority were dropped.
The House received the bill on July 15, 2024, but held it at the desk and never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, which keep the ability to raise dozens of patent claims against biosimilar competitors, and the members who faced no vote they had to explain.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through Senate Judiciary Committee markup and Senate passage.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment in February 2023.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill from the Judiciary Committee to the Senate floor.

for.name: United States Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill by unanimous consent on July 11, 2024, after amending it in the nature of a substitute.

against.name: House of Representatives leadership
against.role: Held the Senate-passed bill at the desk without scheduling a vote
against.what_they_did: Received the Senate-passed bill on July 15, 2024, held it at the desk, and never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by 4 Democrats and 4 Republicans, and passed the Senate by unanimous consent with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill caps the number of patents they can assert against a biosimilar applicant in a single lawsuit, curbing litigation that delays cheaper competition. It does not affect their patents' underlying validity.
Fewer stacked patent claims means less expensive litigation and fewer delays in bringing lower-priced biosimilars to market.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and insurers paying drug prices
industries.note: Faster biosimilar entry would lower the prices they pay, which the bill would facilitate by speeding biosimilar market entry.
